title: Terraform primitives guidance: VPC / IAM / EKS migration playbook
body:
Purpose and scope:
This note captures the recommended interface, variable/output conventions, and an upgrade/migration playbook for our Terraform primitives used in Private deployments (VPC, IAM, cluster primitives for EKS/GKE/AKS). It is intended as a practical handbook for module authors, release engineers, and solution engineers migrating customers between module versions or between cloud/on-prem variants.

Goals and constraints:
- Keep module APIs stable where possible; when breaking changes are necessary, provide explicit migration steps and compatibility helpers.
- Support three deployment contexts: hosted VPC on cloud, VPC connected to customer network (VPN/DirectConnect), and on-prem (air-gapped/air-gated) with limited external access.
- Make it easy to compose primitives (vpc -> iam -> cluster) without duplicating resources or forcing cross-module tight coupling.
- Explicit outputs for consumer modules (applications, platform config) and clear variable names to avoid guesswork.
- Provide tests and upgrade path automation (migration plans in CI).

Module composition and recommended boundaries:
- primitives/vpc : creates the network fabric only (VPC, subnets, IGW/NAT gateways, route tables, GCP/AKS equivalents). No cloud-specific IAM roles.
- primitives/iam : creates foundational roles and policies that are cluster-agnostic (eg. node IAM role, pod-exec role, cross-account trust where applicable).
- primitives/cluster : cluster lifecycle (EKS/GKE/AKS). Depends on vpc and iam primitives but accepts references instead of owning them when requested (see ownership pattern below).
- helpers/outputs-compat : a tiny module used only during upgrade windows to emit old-style output keys mapped from new outputs to keep downstream consumers working.

Ownership patterns and 'accept-or-create' inputs:
To enable composition without resource duplication, each primitive should support an accept-or-create pattern for critical resources:
- vpc module variables: create_vpc (bool), external_vpc_id (string), external_subnet_ids (list). If create_vpc=true, module provisions resources and returns created IDs. If false, module validates required external IDs provided.
- iam module variables: create_iam_roles (bool), node_role_arn (string), oidc_provider_arn (string).
- cluster module variables: create_cluster (bool), vpc_id (string), subnet_ids (list), node_role_arn (string).
This avoids forcing module authors to always own resources. Default should favor create=true for self-contained stacks, but document the mode for managed customer environments.

Variable and output naming conventions (recommended):
- Inputs should be snake_case and prefixed by the resource domain: vpc_cidr_block, vpc_enable_dns_hostnames, eks_cluster_name, gke_node_pool_configs, aks_nodepool_count.
- Outputs should be explicit and stable. Use vendor-neutral names where possible + vendor suffix when necessary. Examples: vpc_id, private_subnet_ids, public_subnet_ids, route_table_ids, nat_gateway_ids, security_group_ids, cluster_kubeconfig, cluster_endpoint, cluster_ca_certificate, oidc_provider_url, node_iam_role_arn, node_instance_profile_id.
- Deprecation rule: when renaming outputs, mark old output as deprecated and still emit it for N releases using helpers/outputs-compat. Add a clear deprecation message in CHANGELOG.

Example variable snippet (Style only, not executable JSON):
- variable "vpc_cidr_block" { type = string default = "10.0.0.0/16" description = "Primary VPC CIDR" }
- variable "private_subnet_cidrs" { type = list(string) default = ["10.0.1.0/24","10.0.2.0/24"] description = "Private subnet CIDRs across AZs" }
- variable "create_vpc" { type = bool default = true description = "If false, expect external_vpc_id and external_subnet_ids" }

Example outputs snippet (Style only):
- output "vpc_id" { value = aws_vpc.main.id description = "VPC id (use this in cluster module)" }
- output "private_subnet_ids" { value = aws_subnet.private[*].id description = "Ordered list of private subnet ids" }
- output "cluster_kubeconfig" { value = local.kubeconfig_raw_sensitive description = "kubeconfig (encoded) for consumption by CI or admin tooling" }

Cluster specifics and cross-cloud considerations:
- EKS: expose outputs for oidc_provider_url, cluster_endpoint, cluster_security_group_id, eks_node_role_arn and kubeconfig. Provide a toggle to provision managed node groups vs. self-managed node ASG/VMs. Support Fargate toggle.
- GKE: expose workload_identity_pool, cluster_ca_certificate, endpoint, and node_pool resource names. GKE will typically own subnet ranges in shared VPCs; support passing shared_vpc mode.
- AKS: expose kube_admin_config and node_resource_group. AKS integrates with AAD; provide variables for AAD integration flags.
- For all: cluster module must accept a kms_key_id for envelope encryption and optional customer-managed KMS/HSM integration for Private deployments.

On-prem / Air-gapped constraints:
- Modules must not rely on remote state downloads during plan/apply in air-gapped mode. Provide a flag air_gapped = true which disables data sources that fetch external metadata and expects necessary inputs passed in.
- Provide a local packaging process (tar.gz of module artifacts and provider plugins) and document how to vendor providers into the private registry.
- Allow explicit endpoint overrides (eg. eks_endpoint_override) for proxy or internal control plane endpoints in hybrid setups.

Versioning and compatibility policy:
- Use semantic versioning for modules. Patch (x.y.z) for bug fixes, minor (x.y+1.0) for additive changes, major (x+1.0.0) for breaking changes.
- For breaking changes, release a migration helper module and a codemod script (terraform state mv helpers) published in redwood-infra/tools.
- Support a three-release overlap: old version -> transitional patch that emits compatibility outputs -> new version where deprecated outputs removed. Document timeline in CHANGELOG and a direct migration checklist in module README.

Upgrade playbook (step-by-step):
1) Pre-flight (local): run terraform plan with NEW_MODULE in a sandbox account. Run static validation: tfsec, checkov, tflint with module rules.
2) Create a branch that pins older module versions used in production to the 'compatibility' branch and add helpers/outputs-compat mapped to new outputs.
3) Smoke deploy in staging: apply new module with create=false when possible and pass in production IDs to validate no unexpected resource replacement.
4) Run state import/state mv steps if resource addresses change. Automate these with scripts and include as a PR checklist item.
5) Monitor the resource replacement list carefully. For NAT, LB, cluster replacement: prefer rolling upgrades (node pool drains, ManagedNodeGroup replace) over full cluster reprovisioning.
6) Run integration tests: cluster creation, app deployment smoke test, networking verification (pod-to-service, egress NAT), and OIDC flows.
7) Final cutover: schedule maintenance window, bump module version in infra repo, apply with canary (subset of stacks), then full rollout.
8) Post-upgrade: keep compatibility outputs active for N releases (document default N=3), remove them only after confirming all consumers migrated.

Testing matrix and CI automation:
- Minimum supported Terraform version: 1.4.6 (override as needed). Provider pins: aws >= 5.0, google >= 4.0, azurerm >= 3.0. Use github actions matrix to test: TF versions x provider versions x module flags (create=true/false x air_gapped true/false).
- Unit tests: terratest or kitchen-terraform suites that validate outputs and no unintended resource replacements.
- Integration tests: ephemeral cluster brings up cluster, runs a simple helm chart, validates egress and node IAM role behavior.

Observability, tagging and tagging policy:
- All resources must accept tags map variable and apply tags to major resources (VPC, subnets, NATs, node groups, roles). Tagging keys: team, cost_center, environment, created_by.
- Emit logs to centralized S3/GCS/Azure blob (configurable), with optional KMS encryption key.

Operational notes and common migration gotchas:
- Changing subnet CIDR or az_count often forces resource replacement; prefer additive subnet strategy where possible.
- Replacing node IAM role will detach instance profiles and require node rotation; coordinate with workloads and use disruption windows.
- OIDC provider changes are usually safe but if thumbprint/thumbprint_list changes, provider must be re-created and pod identity providers can break temporarily.
- When migrating from shared VPC to dedicated VPC or vice versa, validate route propagation and network ACLs carefully.

Delivery checklist for a module release that introduces a breaking change:
- Draft migration doc (short checklist) and include terraform state commands if needed.
- Publish helper module outputs-compat and a yarn/npm/Go binary that wraps state mv commands (in redwood-infra/tools).
- Run the full CI matrix and a staged rollout in one non-production region.
- Announce deprecation window and scheduled removal date to internal consumers and customer-facing SREs.

Appendix: recommended outputs list (stable names)
- vpc_id
- public_subnet_ids
- private_subnet_ids
- route_table_ids
- internet_gateway_id
- nat_gateway_ids
- security_group_ids
- node_iam_role_arn
- node_instance_profile_id
- cluster_endpoint
- cluster_ca_certificate
- cluster_kubeconfig (sensitive, encoded)
- oidc_provider_url
- kms_key_id

Notes for authors: keep README short with examples for the two primary modes: create=true (self-contained) and create=false (reference mode). Include a migration_examples.md that shows terraform state mv commands for common resource moves (subnets, igw, route_tables, node_groups).

Open questions / TODOs:
- Define exact deprecation timeline (default N releases vs team-specific).
- Standardize the name of the helper outputs module across clouds (helpers/outputs-compat vs helpers/output-shims).
- Add a small library that can detect when a plan will replace resources with > 0% downtime and warn in PRs.

Contact and ownership: primaries for this initiative are Priya Shah (module owner), Evan Chen (release automation), Marta Kovacs (test harness). If customers require special migration paths (air-gapped or HSM), involve Solutions Engineering for runbook creation.

End of note.
